final.rationale: I used only variables known at admission and chose an L1-penalized logistic regression with median imputation. The data have 394 events, which is about 10 events per model column for the 35 predictors (39 columns). A penalized model is the safer choice at that ratio. Complete-case analysis would have cut the sample to about half, so I imputed instead. Cross-validated AUC is 0.734 (±0.024) and PR-AUC is 0.543, against 0.232 for a model with no skill. Brier score is 0.144. That is moderate discrimination, not strong. Gradient boosting did no better (AUC 0.723, PR-AUC 0.542), so the signal looks mostly linear and additive. A smaller 23-predictor penalized model gave AUC 0.729 and PR-AUC 0.535, so the extra predictors added little. The main drivers are prior chronic heart failure, which is by far the strongest (OR about 2.15 per SD for stage I), and older age (OR about 1.33 per SD). Lateral MI extent, diabetes, chronic bronchitis, atrial fibrillation on the admission ECG and higher ALT also raise risk. Cardiogenic shock at admission had a lower-than-expected association in this model (OR 0.79 per SD). I did not examine that further, and I would not read it as protective. The odds ratios are standardized, penalized estimates, so they describe association and not causation. The data come from a single hospital in 1992-1995, and I did not validate the model externally. Treat it as a risk-stratification aid and not a precise individual prediction.
